# High-dimensional Procrustes ANOVA

If you have high-dimensional shape data, Procrustes ANOVA to compare group means is probably pretty common. Becuase a Procrustes ANOVA requires a permutation procedure, with thousands of permutations, it can take a long time.

But not all functions are the same! Here we compare several that might be used by researchers who have high-dimensional (HD) shape data: `RRPP::lm.rrpp` & `RRPP::anova.lm.rrpp`, `vegan::adonis2`, and `PERMANOVA::PERMANOVA.`

### Criteria

1.  Single core analysis. Not every function has parallel options, so for functions where it is an option, they will be constrained to use 1 core.
2.  1,000 random permutations. Except in one case we only use 10, and it will be obvious why.
3.  ANOVA must be performed. This means for some functions first fitting many linear models then using `anova()`. Others perform ANOVA inherently.
4.  Data formatting. Any formatting is done prior to analysis but not counted as part of the analysis for measuring computation time.

## Data

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(geomorph)

# make a latticed cube
vert <- 8
template <- expand.grid(1:vert, 1:vert, 1:vert)
colnames(template) <- c("x", "y", "z")

# Groups
ng <- 10
nw <- 10
group <- factor(rep(1:ng, each = nw))
n <- length(group)

# add points for n specimens

LMlist <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(.){
  as.matrix(template + rnorm(length(template),
                   mean = 0, sd = 0.3))
})

```

### GPA

```{r}
LMa <- simplify2array(LMlist)
GPA <- gpagen(LMa, print.progress = FALSE)
plot(GPA)
```

## `RRPP`

```{r}
Y <- two.d.array(GPA$coords)
dim(Y)

system.time(
  {fit1 <- lm.rrpp(Y ~ group, 
                 iter = 999,
                 Parallel = 1,
                 turbo = TRUE);
  AOV1 <- anova(fit1)}
)
AOV1
```

## `vegan`

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(vegan)
D <- dist(Y)
system.time(AOV2 <- adonis2(D ~ group, permutations = 999, parallel = 1))
AOV2
```

## `mvabund`

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(mvabund)
system.time({
  fit3 <- manylm(Y ~ group);
  AOV3 <- anova(fit3, nBoot = 10)
})
AOV3

```

## `PERMANOVA`

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(PERMANOVA)

D2 <- DistContinuous(Y)
system.time(AOV4 <- PERMANOVA(D2, group, nperm = 999))

summary(AOV4)

```

## Initial Conclusions

1.  All results are similar. The `mvabund` $F$-statistics are different because they are like the sum of $p$ $F$-statistics rather than a single $F$-statistic calculated from the sum of $p$ $SS$ values.
2.  `RRPP` and `vegan` are faster than the others.
3.  It probably is not fair to include `mvabund::anova.manylm` because it perfoms more of a MANOVA analysis, which requires inverting residual covariance matrices.
4.  Regardless, `PERMANOVA::PERMANOVA` is comparatively much slower.

## Computation time profiles (increasing $n$)

Let's see how the top two functions (in terms of computational efficiency) perform as we increase the amount of data.

```{r}


nscape <- seq(10, 50, 10)

Result <- sapply(nscape, function(ng){
  group <- factor(rep(1:ng, each = nw))
  n <- length(group)
  LMlist <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(.){
    as.matrix(template + 
                rnorm(length(template),
                mean = 0, sd = 0.3))
  })
  LMa <- simplify2array(LMlist)
  GPA <- gpagen(LMa, 
                print.progress = FALSE)
  Y <- two.d.array(GPA$coords)
  D <- dist(Y)
  df <- rrpp.data.frame(group = group,
                        Y = Y)
  
  t_RRPP <- system.time(
    {fit1 <- lm.rrpp(Y ~ group, 
                     iter = 999,
                     Parallel = 1,
                     turbo = TRUE,
                     data = df);
    AOV1 <- anova(fit1)}
  )[[3]]
  
  t_adonis <- system.time(
    AOV2 <- adonis2(D ~ group,
                    permutations = 999,
                    parallel = 1))[[3]]
  
  c(n = n, t_RRPP = t_RRPP, 
    t_adonis = t_adonis)
  
})

plot(Result[1, ], Result[3,],
     type = "o", pch = 16, col = 2,
     lwd = 2, 
     xlab = "n", ylab = "Time, s")
points(Result[1, ], Result[2,], lwd = 2,
       type = "o", pch = 16, col = 4)
legend("topleft", c("vegan", "RRPP"),
       lty = 1, lwd = 2, 
       pch = 16, col = c(2, 4))
```

This is not surprising because `vegan::adonis2` uses $n \times n$ distance matrices as data and $n \times n$ hat matrices for estimates. Even though it also uses Hadamard products (element-wise products between squared, centered distance and hat matrices), which are computationally quicker than matrix products, the matrices grow exponentially with a linear increase in $n$. By contrast, `RRPP::lm.rrpp` uses sparse-matrix forms of $\mathbf{Q}$ matrices from $\mathbf{QR}$ decomposition of a linear model design matrix, $\mathbf{X}$ and obtains the matrix product, $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Y}$. The sum of squared values from this product is the same as the summed squared values from the Hadamard products, but fewer calculations are needed, especially, comparatively, as $n$ increases.
